text: Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened.
Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
Relate to no one what thou hearest, and reveal to no one what thou seest.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: Accustom thyself to attend carefully to what is said by another, and as much as it is possible, be in the speaker's mind.
No one tests the depth of a river with both his feet.
This Mind in men is God, and for this cause some of mankind are gods, and their humanity is nigh unto divinity.
When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;-- this is knowledge.
The fool has his answer on the edge of his tongue.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Practise piety, with temperance.
Open rebuke is better than secret love.
Be not proud because thou art learned; but discourse with the ignorant man, as with the sage.
Want of sense makes a man the slave of others.
Remember that to change thy opinion and to follow him who corrects thy error is as consistent with freedom as it is to persist in thy error.
Poverty is like honey, it is not peculiar to one place alone.
The best apple is on the highest bough.
Do not have evil-doers for friends, do not have low people for friends: have virtuous people for friends, have for friends the best of men.
He knew nothing, except the fact of his ignorance.
Therefore the sage manages affairs without doing anything, and conveys his instructions without the use of speech.
I am a way to thee a wayfarer.
He that goes among the briers must come out as best he can.
In the land where no wise men are, men of little wit are lords; And the castor-oil's a tree, where no tree else its shade affords.
era: compiled c. 8th-12th c. CE from older material

text: He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city.
For if you once gain time and delay, you will more easily master yourself.
He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.
Quantity makes the cotton draw a stone.
A commander should be daring against his enemy, and kind and good-natured to his own soldiers.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive
Impatience is the sign of a vile and base mind, badly taught and worse accustomed.
source: Sayings of the Ynca Pachacutec (Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries, Bk 6)
era: Inca ruler of the 15th c. CE; recorded c. 1609

text: Lack of knowledge is darker than night.
If any one is punished for a fault, say not that he is punished without reason, lest thou incur the same penalty.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: As is the number of men, so will be the number of purposes.
When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers.
Rather take from the fool, than give to the wise.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Wish to be considered to know nothing; and if you shall seem to some to be a person of importance, distrust yourself.
Where there is no vision, the people perish.
Is virtue a thing remote? I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand.
It is the path you do not fear that the wild beast catches you on.
Your good, careful people of the villages are the thieves of virtue.
A liar findeth sympathy at first, but at the last he is despised and abused.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: Slow but steady wins the race.
source: Aesop, Fables, "The Hare and the Tortoise"

text: As many kinds of wreaths can be made from a heap of flowers, so many good things may be achieved by a mortal when once he is born.
Thy right hand knows nothing of thy left hand.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: If thou wouldest get a friend, prove him first and be not hasty to credit him.
Quarrelling in place of friendship is a foolish thing.
We may then lay down this rule of friendship--neither ask nor consent to do what is wrong.
The Mind, then, is not separated off from God’s essentiality, but is united unto it, as light to sun.
All men are influenced by class-feelings, and there are few who are intelligent.
What the superior man seeks, is in himself. What the mean man seeks, is in others.
It is better for thee to be robbed than to rob thyself.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.
Do not reproach a man with his misfortunes, fearing lest Nemesis may overtake you.
Few men are utterly bad.
When a poor man makes a proverb, it does not spread abroad.
Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet.

Whatever thing, of whatsoever kind it be,
'Tis wisdom's part in each the very thing to see.
An elephant dies, but no one finds his trunk; a tiger dies, but no one finds his stripes.
I obtained life because it was my time: I am now parting with it in accordance with the same law.
What will not wash will not wring.
When thou hast enough, remember the time of hunger: and when thou art rich, think upon poverty and need.
To rule one’s tongue, especially at a banquet, and not to speak ill of one’s neighbours; for if one does so one is sure to hear what one will not like.
If thy neighbour dislike thee, change the gate of thy house.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: When one stands on another's shoulders, then he sees over the market.
This: As long as you talked, so long I quietly heard.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: Small knowledge has not the compass of great knowledge any more than a short year has the length of a long year.
Whatever a hater may do to a hater, or an enemy to an enemy, a wrongly-directed mind will do us greater mischief.
To have faults and not to reform them,-- this, indeed, should be pronounced having faults.
The grass which you disregard will injure your eye.
Take away thy opinion, and then there is taken away the complaint, "I have been harmed." Take away the complaint, "I have been harmed," and the harm is taken away.
He that can rule his tongue shall live without strife; and he that hateth babbling shall have less evil.
For where is Soul, there too is Mind; just as where Life, there is there also Soul.
Nothing for me is too early nor too late, which is in due time for thee.
The journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
And he who has pleasure in the Living One, will himself become living.
It was more princely to add than to take away.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Artaxerxes I
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text:
Fierceness in hour of strife heroic greatness shows;
Its edge is kindness to our suffering foes.
A little hole will sink a big ship.
Kick away the ladder and the legs are left swinging.
If one man does not know, another man explains.
A good name is better than precious ointment.
No evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
The superior man wishes to be slow in his speech and earnest in his conduct.
As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.
The rejoicing of the envious rends the heart.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses.
When riches are gained, follow the heart; for riches are of no avail if one be weary.
Every foot will tread on him who is in the mud.
Let us rejoice now, dear friends and children, for life is not long upon earth.
The enmity of the wise, rather than the friendship of the fool.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Who is content needs fear no shame.
The legs of one man are no good to another for walking.
Live, therefore, in the house of kindliness, and men shall come and give gifts of themselves.
Fools follow after vanity, men of evil wisdom. The wise man keeps earnestness as his best jewel.
The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.
You might just as well take the sun out of the sky as friendship from life; for the immortal gods have given us nothing better or more delightful.
Keep a sweet tongue and open thy mouth to speak what is good.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: Necessity is the strongest of things, for it rules everything
The cure for a conflagration is to have two houses.
There are few in the world who attain to the teaching without words, and the advantage arising from non-action.

Nothing exists, save wealth, that can
Change man of nought to worthy man.
To repent in time is gain, but to repent too late is useless.
The Spartans do not enquire how many the enemy are, but where they are.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: If fierce anger seize thee, say not a word, lest thou be called senseless.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: When things have become strong, they (then) become old, which may be said to be contrary to the Tao.
The big calabash of honour is better than one of punishment.
He that promises most will perform least.
For where is day, nowhere is night; and where is night, day is nowhere.
Constant action overcomes cold; being still overcomes heat. Purity and stillness give the correct law to all under heaven.
Envy is a worm that gnaws and consumes the entrails of the envious.
source: Sayings of the Ynca Pachacutec (Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries, Bk 6)
era: Inca ruler of the 15th c. CE; recorded c. 1609

text: Forbear to speak evil not only of your friends, but also of your enemies.
As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.
Riches have disclosed in thy character the bad qualities formerly concealed by thy poverty.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
Now therefore he who understandeth, let him understand.
Only honorable things are honorable, and only just things are just.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Antigonus
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: By and by comes the Great Awakening, and then we find out that this life is really a great dream.
A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches.
No one dreams of going to where they will kill him.

The worthy say, when wealth rewards their toil-spent hours,
For uses of beneficence alone 'tis ours.
It is a man’s own opinions which disturb him.
The fact is that the blame for all complaints of that kind is to be charged to character, not to a particular time of life.
The firm, the enduring, the simple, and the modest are near to virtue.
Fire when small is a friend, but when large it is an enemy.

With plans not well matured to rise against your foe,
Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow!
Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof: and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
Water does not get bitter without a cause.
Venture not on the road with a man who will not accept advice, and sit not down at the same table with a deceiver.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: The difficulty, my friends, is not to avoid death, but to avoid unrighteousness; for that runs faster than death.
Fair speech is more rare than the emerald that is found by slave-maidens on the pebbles.
The relation of the Tao to all the world is like that of the great rivers and seas to the streams from the valleys.
Be not over sweet, lest they eat thee up, nor over bitter, lest thy friends run away from thee.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: The man of one cow will sometimes want milk.
The dog does not bark in his own house.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: It is good to tame the mind, which is difficult to hold in and flighty, rushing wherever it listeth; a tamed mind brings happiness.
Give thyself time to learn something new and good, and cease to be whirled around.
Æon is, then, in God; Cosmos, in Æon; in Cosmos, Time; in Time, Becoming.
Though rain beats on a stone it (the stone) stands firm where it stands.
For we are all, one with another, wise and foolish, like a ring which has no end.
May not the space between heaven and earth be compared to a bellows?
There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death.
It is not the eye that understands, but the mind.
When the belly is full, then the eye waxes dull.
The highest excellence is like (that of) water.
My father bequeathed to me his government, but not his fortune.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Dionysius the Younger
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: The guest of the hospitable treats hospitably.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Hold your tongues, lest they should find out that you are in this ship.
Long is the night to him who is awake; long is a mile to him who is tired; long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law.
The pure men of old did not know what it was to love life or to hate death.
It is the Good which doeth the creating.
He, O men, is the wisest, who, like Socrates, knows that his wisdom is in truth worth nothing
The flower is worn in the ear, but the stalk is cast aside.
Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.
No one knows what the elephant ate to make it big.

The men of lofty mind quail not in ruin's fateful hour,
The elephant retains his dignity mid arrows' deadly shower.
Therefore did the wise sovereigns of antiquity seek the man to fill the office, and not the office for the sake of the man.
It is virtue, virtue, which both creates and preserves friendship.
He who lies in the mud will rise dirty.
Take up no quarrel with a man stronger than thyself; thou canst not know how he will pounce on thee.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: He that kills another without authority or just cause, condemns himself to death.
source: Sayings of the Ynca Pachacutec (Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries, Bk 6)
era: Inca ruler of the 15th c. CE; recorded c. 1609

text: He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty.
He who eats the jack-fruit will get his fingers sticky.
Time is the wisest of things, for it finds out everything.
All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
If so little a creature will oppose injurious violence, what think ye that men ought to do?
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: By the time the fool has learned to play the game, the players have dispersed.
The great Tao (or way) is very level and easy; but people love the by-ways.
The eye-witness observes what the absent does not see.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: If a man in the morning hear the right way, he may die in the evening without regret.
Better thine own work is, though done with fault, than doing others' work, ev'n excellently.
If thou hast wealth, do not allow thyself to be tormented by hunger or thirst.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: A knave for one is a good man for another.
A cup of water quencheth the thirst, and a mouthful of melon supporteth the heart.
That which is crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.
Seek excess in nothing.
It is better for him to die than to live, who must be weary not only of his enemies, but of his friends too.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Dion
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: (The words from) the mouth of an old man are better than any amulet.
Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?
The eyes close in sleep, but the pillow remains awake.
While the hungry lion slumbers, not a deer comes to his den.
era: compiled c. 8th-12th c. CE from older material

text: A merry heart doeth good like a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones.
Two never agreed at the kindling of a fire.
Wherefore we ought to put away verbosity and foolish talk, and understand these two—the made and Maker.
I’ll show that it is not the places that grace men, but men the places.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: The man who despises the law goes towards his fall, but the just man will rise higher.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: For regulating the human (in our constitution) and rendering the (proper) service to the heavenly, there is nothing like moderation.
For nothing inspires love, nothing conciliates affection, like virtue.
However long the neck is, the head is above it.
You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,--the creature of a season.

Unenduring is all wealth; if you wealth enjoy,
Enduring works in working wealth straightway employ.
Repeat not extravagant speech, neither listen thereto; for it is the utterance of a body heated by wrath.
The noble and generous man is known by the patience he shows in adversity.
source: Sayings of the Ynca Pachacutec (Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries, Bk 6)
era: Inca ruler of the 15th c. CE; recorded c. 1609

text: Expel avidity from thy heart; the fetters will be loosened from thy foot.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: To go beyond is as wrong as to fall short.
Do good unto thy friend before thou die, and according to thy ability stretch out thy hand and give to him.
Before long, alas! this body will lie on the earth, despised, without understanding, like a useless log.
Example is more powerful than precept.
source: Aesop, Fables, "The Crab and Its Mother"

text: Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts.
Little fishes are the prey of large ones.
I am a door to thee who knockest at Me.
' Friend, friend (I will tell you a secret),' that is how news spreads.
Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of movement.
Such friendship enhances prosperity, and relieves adversity of its burden by halving and sharing it.
Who gives not thanks to men, gives not thanks to God.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text:
Who daring climbs, and would himself upraise
Beyond the branch's tip, with life the forfeit pays.
Be not fain to trample on thy neighbour, lest the like happen to thyself.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: It is a small thing that is taken to measure a big thing.
The man that went farthest from home had as far to come back.
All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left hand and on the right.
A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.
Power shows the man.

If each his own, as neighbours' faults would scan,
Could any evil hap to living man?
There is no Good that can be got from objects in the world.
Enough for you to receive, but not for me to give.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Alexander
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: The favorites of kings sometimes can do every thing with them, sometimes little or nothing.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Orontes
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: The heart knoweth his own bitterness; and a stranger doth not intermeddle with his joy.
Stretch your legs according to the length of your blanket.
Learn as if you could not reach your object, and were always fearing also lest you should lose it.
One volunteer is worth ten pressed men.
To avoid excess in everything.
Man takes his law from the Earth; the Earth takes its law from Heaven; Heaven takes its law from the Tao. The law of the Tao is its being what it is.
The meanest person in the house brags most of his kindred.
Strive to continue to be such as philosophy wished to make thee.
The Egyptian kings, according unto their law, used to swear their judges that they should not obey the king when he commanded them to give an unjust sentence.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Egyptian Kings
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: As rain breaks through an ill-thatched house, passion will break through an unreflecting mind.
The cautious seldom err.
As in water face answereth to face, so the heart of man to man.
No one knows the story of to-morrow's dawn.
Who knocks at the door will hear the answer.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Most men are wicked.
If a man take no thought about what is distant, he will find sorrow near at hand.
Yea, understand the Cosmos is by God and in God; but Man by Cosmos and in Cosmos.
If thy house be too high, make the walls lower, and then walk in.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not.

The furtive glance, that gleams one instant bright,
Is more than half of love's supreme delight.
To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
What one people talk and laugh about, another people talk and cry about.
Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
Everything is only for a day, both that which remembers and that which is remembered.
He who is at his ease does not know what it is to be in want.
You can be invincible, if you enter into no contest in which it is not in your power to conquer.
If thou drink wine, speak little.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: Cut up the evil by the root.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text:
Although you hate incur of those whose ploughs are bows,
Make not the men whose ploughs are words your foes!
He that waits long at the ferry will get over some time.
One Passion hath God only—Good; and He who’s Good, is neither arrogant nor impotent.
In ancient times, men learned with a view to their own improvement. Now-a-days, men learn with a view to the approbation of others.
Whether we will be well or ill spoken of is in our own power.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Philip
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: In this world, few are born with knowledge: wisdom is the product of earnest meditation.
Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
The man with a covering shivers, the naked man pins his faith to a fire.
The superior man is catholic and no partisan. The mean man is partisan and not catholic.
Do not say before hand what you are going to do; for if you fail, you will be laughed at.
On the day of victory no fatigue is felt.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Silence is more profitable unto thee than abundance of speech.
If there is no wind the trees do not rock.
Well-makers lead the water (wherever they like); fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.
However hard a thing is thrown into the air it always falls to the ground.
Better no ring than a rush ring.
I had rather be called merciful a great while, than lord a little while.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Philip
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: The reason why the ancients did not readily give utterance to their words, was that they feared lest their actions should not come up to them.
If a fool be associated with a wise man even all his life, he will perceive the truth as little as a spoon perceives the taste of soup.
Let us be happy in the present, for life is transitory.
Even the Gods cannot strive against necessity.
Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.
A friend who dwells near thee is better than a brother far off.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: The superior man is affable, but not adulatory; the mean man is adulatory, but not affable.
To have patience with a friend rather than lose him for ever.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: From fear of losing a drop the whole is spilt.
He that is most unlike thee.
source: Plutarch, Laconic Apophthegms: Agis the Younger
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: I am a lamp to thee who seest Me.
Their right is our wrong, and our right is their wrong.
For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
Always bear this in mind; and another thing too, that very little indeed is necessary for living a happy life.
He who hazards not will neither lose nor win.
Nothing doth countervail a faithful friend, and his excellency is invaluable.
One only seeks a guide when one has lost the road.
The mind of the superior man is conversant with righteousness; the mind of the mean man is conversant with gain.
A grease stain is more lasting than one of water.
The soft overcomes the hard; and the weak the strong.
But where there’s passion, nowhere is there Good; and where is Good, nowhere a single passion.
Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
If thou be powerful, make thyself to be honoured for knowledge and for gentleness.
In quarreling about the shadow we often lose the substance.
source: Aesop, Fables, "The Ass and His Shadow"

text: If the nose is cut off the face is disfigured.
It is better that others should envy you for being good, than that you should envy others, you yourself being evil.
source: Sayings of the Ynca Pachacutec (Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries, Bk 6)
era: Inca ruler of the 15th c. CE; recorded c. 1609

text: It is one man who kills an elephant, but many people who eat its flesh.
For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.
Virtue is not left to stand alone. He who practises it will have neighbors.
When a man distinguishes himself, worry him not; if a mishap occur to him, rejoice not over it.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: Vice must be drawn out, that virtue may remain.
Courage would be good for nothing, if there were no justice; and if all men were just, there would be no need of courage.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: By nature, men are nearly alike; by practice, they get to be wide apart.

Man's fitting work is known but by success achieved;
In midst the plan revealed brings ruin ne'er to be retrieved.
The earth could not bear two suns, nor Asia two kings.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Alexander
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: Short cuts often lead into mire.
When the fool is told a proverb, the meaning of it has to be explained to him.
Ask assistance from those only who have the power of helping thee.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Well, it is a glory for one that hath abundance to live as reason not as appetite directs.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly.
Misery!--happiness is to be found by its side! Happiness!--misery lurks beneath it! Who knows what either will come to in the end?
Consult not with a fool; for he cannot keep counsel.
There never was a man trained to righteousness who made his ruler an after consideration.
A good case is not difficult to state.
Prove thy friend first with bread and wine, then may he be admitted to something better.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: The pupil of the eye cannot be separated from the white.
I am a mirror to thee who understandest Me.
What great wonder is it, that in four years they can be just one day?
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: He that hears badly will answer badly.
The superior man is satisfied and composed; the mean man is always full of distress.
A thing that does not satiate, creates hunger.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: A modest manner fits a maid, And Patience is a man's adorning.
era: compiled c. 8th-12th c. CE from older material

text: Watch your opportunity.
For he that is joined to Him that is immortal, will also himself become immortal.
Nobody ought to govern, unless he was better than those he governed.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Cyrus
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text:
With stronger than thyself, turn from the strife away;
With weaker shun not, rather court the fray.
Great is Truth, appointing a straight path.
Wealth is a fine thing, but to find an heir is not easy.
He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it.
Pride goes before destruction.
source: Aesop, Fables, "The Fighting Cocks and the Eagle"

text: A friend cannot be known in prosperity: and an enemy cannot be hidden in adversity.
Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.
Love that only which happens to thee and is spun with the thread of thy destiny.

Man's wisdom seems the offspring of his mind;
'Tis outcome of companionship we find.
Pardon is better than punishment.
The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
Evil knows the sleeping place of evil.
The dead tree falls and the woodpecker perishes with it.
I unwind my song like a string of precious jewels.
Every thing crooked-necked is not a camel.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Judge uprightly and thou wilt be honoured in thine old age.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them.
To rebel against nature--is not that to fight like the giants with the gods?
The first story from the host, and tales till morning from the guest.

Let king search out his servants' deeds each day;
When these do right, the world goes rightly on its way.
One does not speak out one's mind in the presence of a chief, but behind his back one does.
Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth.
For naught is like to That which hath no like, and is Alone and One.
I don’t think that shoemaker a good workman that makes a great shoe for a little foot.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: The wise are free from perplexities; the virtuous from anxiety; and the bold from fear.
If thou say a good word for thy friend before the judge, thou hast snatched a lamb out of the jaws of the lion.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: Chastise that which is evil and encourage that which is good.
Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
Faults are like a hill, you mount on your own and then see other people's.

In nature's way who spends his calm domestic days,
'Mid all that strive for virtue's crown hath foremost place.
What makes a great state is its being (like) a low-lying, down-flowing (stream).
That which is not good for the swarm, neither is it good for the bee.
One cannot both feast and become rich.
Let right deeds be thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them.
The one-eyed person is a beauty in the country of the blind.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Well then, man: do what nature now requires.
Who knows to stop Incurs no blame. From danger free Long live shall he.
A child is known by his manners.
Do you, O Thales, who cannot see what is under your feet, think that you shall understand what is in heaven?
Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
I have carried salt and have removed lead; and I have not seen anything heavier than that a man should pay a debt that he did not borrow.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins.
Where there are no eagles, the grasshoppers say we are eagles.
You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,--the creature of a narrower sphere.
Suit thy business to thy circumstances.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: The seeds of God, ’tis true, are few, but vast and fair, and good—virtue and self-control, devotion.
Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good.
They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it, and they who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
When a chief has plenty of milk, then all people drink of him.
An evil deed, like newly-drawn milk, does not turn (suddenly); smouldering, like fire covered by ashes, it follows the fool.
A clean corner is not the worse of being searched.
He that obeyeth becometh one obeyed.
If you pat a dog on the head, he wags his tail.
Those who seek to please everybody please nobody.
source: Aesop, Fables, "The Man and His Two Sweethearts"

text: As to the people, if they have not a certain livelihood, they will be found not to have a fixed heart.
Being thin is not dying.
I myself am master of my words, but the king and fortune have power over my actions.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Siramnes
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: In the face of a true friend a man sees as it were a second self.
The Glory of all things is God, Godhead and Godly Nature.

Let those that need partake your meal; guard everything that lives:
This the chief and sum of lore that hoarded wisdom gives.
A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
Let us cease from wrath, and refrain from angry looks.
Intellect is the swiftest of things, for it runs through everything
No limit can be set to skill, neither is there any craftsman that possesseth full advantages.
If the people be led by laws, and uniformity sought to be given them by punishments, they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame.
The embrace at meeting is better than that at parting.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: When a bird remains too long on a tree, it has a stone thrown at it.
All men know the use of useful things; but they do not know the use of useless things.
Suretyship, and then destruction.
Change not a friend for any good by no means; neither a faithful brother for the gold of Ophir.
Be not hard, like the bones of men, nor soft as a sponge.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: He that envies and is envied, has a double torment.
source: Sayings of the Ynca Pachacutec (Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries, Bk 6)
era: Inca ruler of the 15th c. CE; recorded c. 1609

text: The progress of the superior man is upwards; the progress of the mean man is downwards.
He who is always angry is of nature like the bramble.
Misfortune tests the sincerity of friends.
source: Aesop, Fables, "The Bear and the Two Travelers"

text:
Of all good things we 've scanned with studious care,
There 's nought that can with truthfulness compare.
It sometimes happens that the man who plants the cocoa-nut does not eat of its fruit.
A threefold cord is not quickly broken.
When one would climb a tree, one begins from the bottom and not from the top.
Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting.
If an intelligent man be associated for one minute only with a wise man, he will soon perceive the truth, as the tongue perceives the taste of soup.
He who requires much from himself and little from others, will keep himself from being the object of resentment.
If I have done any brave action, that will preserve my memory; if not, neither will a thousand statues, the works of base mechanics.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text:
Men are not one because their members seem alike to outward view;
Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true.
Every one knows best his own affairs, and those interested in them.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Now therefore he who hath ear to hear let him hear.
Seeing is better than hearing.
A faithfull friend is a strong defence: and he that hath found such an one hath found a treasure.
The unexamined life is not worth living
If thou hast a wound on thy foot, step not forth firmly.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: Fine words and an insinuating appearance are seldom associated with true virtue.
Better that you should be made to wait for food than that food should be made to wait for you.

Pleasant words are words with all pervading love that burn;
Words from his guileless mouth who can the very truth discern.
He who exercises government by means of his virtue may be compared to the north polar star, which keeps its place and all the stars turn towards it.
The nurse is kissed for the sake of the child.
Do not beat the wolf, and do not cause hunger to the sheep.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: Keep silence on My Mysteries.
Look at things again as thou didst use to look at them; for in this consists the recovery of thy life.
You then, when you are silent, are worth nothing.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: Stratagem is better than brute force.
A man can enlarge the principles which he follows; those principles do not enlarge the man.
I take this for a wise man, who chose rather to commit himself to a good man than to a strong place.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Alexander
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.

Friendship of fools is very pleasant thing;
Parting with them will leave behind no sting.
The early riser will beat the late watcher.
You reign over the Macedonians, men that have learned fighting; and I over the Scythians, which can fight with hunger and thirst.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Ateas
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: Sparrows with sparrows and hornbills with hornbills.
If thou be among people, make for thyself love, the beginning and end of the heart.
Working out one's allotted span, and not perishing in mid career,--this is the fulness of knowledge.
Judge none blessed before his death: for a man shall be known in his children.
Good faith is the foundation of right.
But if a man's ears are so closed to plain speaking that he cannot bear to hear the truth from a friend, we may give him up in despair.
There are three things worth having in this world, courage, good sense, and caution.
When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
He who is not ashamed does whatever he likes.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: The fact is that fewer people are endowed with virtue than wish to be thought to be so.
When you have caught the mother hen, you pick up the chickens without difficulty.
That friend only is the true friend who is near when trouble comes; That man only is the brave man who can bear the battle-drums.
era: compiled c. 8th-12th c. CE from older material

text: Man is born for uprightness. If a man lose his uprightness, and yet live, his escape from death is the effect of mere good fortune.
The rumour is better than the reality.
Those who suffer most cry out the least.
source: Aesop, Fables, "The Oxen and the Axle-Trees"

text: It is better to listen to a wise man when he is drunk than to a noodle when he is sober.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text:
A tongue that rightly speaks the right is greatest gain,
It stands alone midst goodly things that men obtain.
Be wise and understanding and vigilant.
Short is the little which remains to thee of life.
Whoever catches a hare has to run for it.
The talents of a person are less admired at home than abroad.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: A man whose toes have been cut off does not value a present of boots.
Earnestness is the path of immortality (Nirvana), thoughtlessness the path of death.
Those who want fewest things are nearest to the Gods.
The fool of forty will never be wise.
The accomplished scholar is not a utensil.
If thou hast understanding, answer thy neighbour; if not, lay thy hand upon thy mouth.
Men, of course, who have no resources in themselves for securing a good and happy life find every age burdensome.
For Gnosis of the Good is holy silence and a giving holiday to every sense.
For lack of asking prices bargains are lost.
Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord?
Heedlessness leadeth unto disobedience on the morrow; but understanding shall stablish him.
The man who knows not how to govern his house and family, will know much less how to rule a state.
source: Sayings of the Ynca Pachacutec (Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries, Bk 6)
era: Inca ruler of the 15th c. CE; recorded c. 1609

text: Better is he that laboureth, and aboundeth in all things, than he that boasteth himself, and wanteth bread.
Nothing happens to any man which he is not formed by nature to bear.
The perception of what is small is (the secret of) clear-sightedness; the guarding of what is soft and tender is (the secret of) strength.
The mouth brings honey and the tail carries a sting.
If thou wert not a wicked person and of insatiable covetousness, thou wouldst not disturb the mansions of the dead.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Semiramis
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: It is one thing to live with a tyrant, another with a friend.
Therefore that knowledge which stops at what it does not know, is the highest knowledge.
When you follow behind your father, you learn to walk like him.
Mud may be wiped, but wise men plunge not in it.
era: compiled c. 8th-12th c. CE from older material

text: The bowman hitteth the mark, as the steersman reacheth land, by diversity of aim.
The eye is not a measure, but it knows what is small.
Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend.
Good sir, be not concerned that you must leave the city, but that you have left justice.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: He that envies another, injures himself.
source: Sayings of the Ynca Pachacutec (Garcilaso de la Vega, Royal Commentaries, Bk 6)
era: Inca ruler of the 15th c. CE; recorded c. 1609

text: When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.
Who danceth not, knows not what is being done.
The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.
For there should be no satiety in friendship, as there is in other things.
The moon is none the worse of the dogs’ barking at her.
To be poor without murmuring is difficult. To be rich without being proud is easy.
Times are so bad that even Pharaoh is regretted.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: There is no medicine to cure hatred.
But friendship by its nature admits of no feigning, no pretence: as far as it goes it is both genuine and spontaneous.
It is better to die with a good name than to live with a bad one.
Both the seeds of plants and the lives of men resemble the soil they inhabit.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Cyrus
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
In a country there are not two lords; the people have not two masters.
That deed is not well done of which a man must repent, and the reward of which he receives crying and with a tearful face.
The friend in need is the only friend.
In God alone, is, therefore, Good, or rather Good is God Himself.
A man’s pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit.
I neither know nor think that I know.
Advice given in the midst of a crowd is loathsome.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: If the will be set on virtue, there will be no practice of wickedness.
It is a shame, Athenians, that those who were once the lords of all Greece should understand what is right and just less than the people of Megara.
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: If one could not make use of gold dust, then it would merely be called sand.

Many wash in hallowed waters, living lives of hidden shame;
Foul in heart, yet high upraised of men in virtuous fame.
Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.
If thou hast no horse of thine own, ride not on a strange one; if it becomes lame, thou wilt be laughed at.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: The eye of the sun cannot be hidden.
source: Arabic Proverbs (collected at Cairo by Burckhardt)

text: And the soul’s vice is ignorance.
Fishes should not be taken from the deep; instruments for the profit of a state should not be shown to the people.
He is wise who is warned by the misfortunes of others.
AVhen you do not know how to dance, then you say, ' The drum is not sounding sweetly'.
My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit.
Sentences of studied wisdom, nought avail they unapplied; Though the blind man hold a lantern, yet his footsteps stray aside.
era: compiled c. 8th-12th c. CE from older material

text: Those I made first, but now I make these by my valor and industry.
source: Plutarch, Apophthegms of Kings and Great Commanders: Agathocles
translator: Several hands, ed. W. W. Goodwin, 1878

text: Whosoever digs a pit he shall fall into it himself.
It is because of to-morrow that one cleans up at night.
The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like [the wrong-doer].
Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour.
If thou hast no bodily hunger, eat not bread, lest thou appear greedy.
source: Story of Ahikar (sayings of Ahikar, composite versions)
era: sage of the 7th c. BCE (versions later)
translator: F. C. Conybeare, J. R. Harris, A. S. Lewis, 1913

text: A man laments not what he does not see.
Moderation is the best thing.
Give mean men power, and give thy throat to the knife; The Mouse, made Tiger, sought his master's life.
era: compiled c. 8th-12th c. CE from older material

text: The Tao in its regular course does nothing (for the sake of doing it), and so there is nothing which it does not do.
Be not covetous toward thy neighbours; for with a gentle man praise availeth more than might.
